shared.concept_anchor: Limitations — non-exhaustive list, citizen-only, non-justiciable

en.display_text:
With reference to the limitations and scope of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A of the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:

1. The list of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A is non-exhaustive in that it omits several civic obligations — such as a duty to vote or pay taxes — which are found in the constitutions of some other democracies.
2. Fundamental Duties under Article 51A bind only citizens of India and do not extend to foreign nationals or corporations, limiting their scope relative to some Fundamental Rights.
3. Since Fundamental Duties cannot be enforced through judicial proceedings, Parliament has no constitutional authority to enact laws that penalise conduct violating a Fundamental Duty.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 only
(b) 3 only
(c) 1 and 2 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3

statement_analysis.statement: The list of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A is non-exhaustive in that it omits several civic obligations — such as a duty to vote or pay taxes — which are found in the constitutions of some other democracies.
statement_analysis.reason: The Swaran Singh Committee recommended a duty to pay taxes, but it was not enacted. No duty to vote appears in Article 51A. Constitutions of other democracies include such civic duties.

statement_analysis.statement: Fundamental Duties under Article 51A bind only citizens of India and do not extend to foreign nationals or corporations, limiting their scope relative to some Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 51A's explicit 'every citizen of India' language excludes non-citizens and corporations. By contrast, rights under Articles 14 and 21 extend to all 'persons'.

statement_analysis.statement: Since Fundamental Duties cannot be enforced through judicial proceedings, Parliament has no constitutional authority to enact laws that penalise conduct violating a Fundamental Duty.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliament's legislative power is separate from Article 51A's non-justiciability. Multiple statutes (Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, Wildlife Protection Act) effectively enforce Fundamental Duties through penal provisions.

en.strong_distractor: d — '1, 2 and 3' is appealing to students who assume non-justiciability is a comprehensive bar on enforcement, including by Parliament.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: Article 51A omits voting and tax duties — well-documented limitations confirmed by comparing with Swaran Singh's unimplemented recommendations.
Statement 2 is correct: Citizen-only scope is confirmed by Article 51A's opening language — a genuine limitation relative to rights like Articles 14 and 21.
Statement 3 is incorrect: Parliament retains full authority to legislate — non-justiciability bars direct writ enforcement only. Existing statutes already penalise duty-violating conduct.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, Statement 3 is incorrect — select option (c).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a partial-truth trap: it correctly states that Fundamental Duties cannot be enforced through judicial proceedings (writ jurisdiction), but incorrectly extends this to bar parliamentary legislation. The error is conflating constitutional non-justiciability with a bar on Parliament's legislative power to enforce duty-aligned conduct. These operate on entirely different planes of constitutional law.
en.final_explanation:
The limitations of Fundamental Duties as enacted reveal important gaps in India's civic duty framework.

• Statement 1 — Correct: No duty to vote or pay taxes is found in Article 51A, despite these being fundamental civic obligations in many democracies. The Swaran Singh Committee recommended the tax duty; Parliament did not enact it.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The citizen-exclusivity of Fundamental Duties is a textual limitation. Non-citizens and corporations are exempt, whereas some rights (Articles 14, 20, 21) extend universally to persons.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Parliament is fully empowered to legislate on any subject giving effect to Fundamental Duties. The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971) and Wildlife Protection Act (1972) are examples of penal statutes reinforcing duties. Non-justiciability of Article 51A itself does not constrain Parliament's Article 246 legislative power.

Value Addition:
• The Verma Committee (1999) recommended making duties more effective through existing legislation — not new duty-specific statutes.
• Jury duty, community service, and compulsory national service are examples of civic duties in other constitutions absent from Article 51A.
• Duties apply to natural persons who are citizens — NRIs holding OCI cards are not citizens and thus not subject to Article 51A.

hi.display_text:
भारत के संविधान के अनुच्छेद 51A के अंतर्गत मौलिक कर्तव्यों की सीमाओं और दायरे के संदर्भ में, निम्नलिखित कथनों पर विचार करें:

1. अनुच्छेद 51A के अंतर्गत मौलिक कर्तव्यों की सूची अपूर्ण है क्योंकि इसमें कई नागरिक दायित्व शामिल नहीं हैं — जैसे मतदान करने या कर देने का कर्तव्य — जो कुछ अन्य लोकतंत्रों के संविधान में पाए जाते हैं।
2. अनुच्छेद 51A के अंतर्गत मौलिक कर्तव्य केवल भारत के नागरिकों को बाध्य करते हैं और विदेशी नागरिकों या निगमों पर लागू नहीं होते, जिससे इनके दायरे की तुलना कुछ मौलिक अधिकारों से सीमित होती है।
3. चूंकि मौलिक कर्तव्यों को न्यायिक कार्यवाही के माध्यम से लागू नहीं किया जा सकता, इसलिए संसद के पास ऐसे कर्तव्य का उल्लंघन करने वाले आचरण को दंडित करने वाले कानून बनाने का संवैधानिक अधिकार नहीं है।

उपरोक्त में से कौन-सा/से कथन सही है/हैं?

(a) केवल 1
(b) केवल 3
